Calling al-Fārābī an Arab philosopher does not conflict with the fact that he was of Turkic—or, according to some historians, Persian—origin. As ʿUthmān Amīn rightly says, al-Fārābī “was an Arab philosopher in the totality of his culture and writings” (ʿUthmān Amīn, introduction to al-Fārābī’s Enumeration of the Sciences, 3rd ed., p. 38).↩︎

Al-Fārābī defines philosophy as “knowledge of existing things insofar as they exist” (The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages, Beirut, 2nd ed., ed. Albert Naṣrī Nādir, 1968, p. 80; and The Pleasant Fruit: Selected Treatises of al-Fārābī, Dieterici ed., Leiden, 1890, pp. 1–2). Al-Fārābī regards philosophy as the foremost of all sciences because it makes existing things intelligible through certain demonstrations (Attainment of Happiness, Hyderabad ed., 1345 AH, p. 36).↩︎

The ideological character of philosophy—of every philosophy—is an objective fact. It does not depend on whether the philosopher is aware of it, nor on whether we recognize it in one philosopher or another. Like every other form of human consciousness, philosophy has no history separate from the history of real people living under particular economic and social conditions. In every society and every age, philosophy therefore presents a system of ideas about the world in which the character of the prevailing social relations and the ideological struggle within those relations are indirectly reflected. Through these ideas, philosophy also defines each philosopher’s position within that struggle.↩︎

Medieval Arab philosophers knew the work called Theology as The Theology of Aristotle or Aristotle’s Book of Divinity. The mistaken attribution to Aristotle may have arisen because the work, whose author was then unknown, reached them together with explanations by Porphyry of Tyre, whom they knew as a commentator on Aristotle. They therefore assumed that the work itself was by Aristotle. ʿAbd al-Masīḥ ibn ʿAbd Allāh ibn Nāʿima al-Ḥimṣī (d. 220 AH/835 CE) translated it into Arabic, and al-Kindī revised the translation. Dieterici first published it in Berlin in 1882, and it was translated into Latin in 1519. In reality, the work is drawn from the Fourth and Sixth Enneads of Plotinus. See ʿAbd al-Raḥmān Badawī’s edition of the Fourth Ennead, On the Soul, Cairo, 1970, pp. 156–157.↩︎

The Arabic historical sources that record the translation movement under the early and later Abbasids all testify to this. Examples include Ibn al-Nadīm’s Fihrist (pp. 263, 348, 411), al-Qifṭī’s Accounts of the Scholars (pp. 118, 122, 130, 266, and elsewhere), and Ibn Abī Uṣaybiʿa’s Classes of Physicians (vol. 1, p. 235; vol. 2, p. 335, and elsewhere). Modern historians and researchers—Arab, Eastern, and Orientalist alike—have likewise reached the conclusion, through their studies and textual research, that this historical fact is sound: the Arab philosophers knew Aristotle’s philosophy.↩︎

Al-Fārābī contradicts himself on this point. His entire philosophical system is built on emanation, which necessarily rules out creation from nothing and implies the eternity of the world; this is also what the meaning of his philosophical texts themselves requires. Yet in The Harmonization of the Opinions of the Two Sages (same edition, pp. 100–104), he says that God brought the world into existence from nothing (pp. 101, 103, 104), and that the world came into being. He even calls the belief that Aristotle held the world to be eternal “an ugly and objectionable supposition” (p. 100). How should we understand this contradiction, and which of al-Fārābī’s two positions should we accept? In our view, the contradiction is apparent rather than real. It was a means of self-protection—a method Arab-Islamic philosophers of the period allowed themselves to use to an unreasonable degree. Their real views are those embodied in their philosophical theories, not the statements they make outside those theories. Otherwise their entire philosophical systems would become meaningless.↩︎

Ibid., p. 74. It should be noted that al-Fārābī understands the relation between matter and form in existing things in the Aristotelian way. When a particular form belongs to a particular matter, the form is not always absolutely form, nor is the matter always absolutely matter. A form can be form in relation to what lies below it and matter in relation to what lies above it. In the same way, matter can be matter in relation to what lies above it and form in relation to what lies below it. In the present case, al-Fārābī says that the imaginative faculty is matter in relation to what stands above it, namely the rational faculty. The rational faculty, in turn, is form in relation to the imaginative faculty because it stands above it. The rational faculty remains form, since no faculty of the soul stands above it. This is what he means when he says: “It is the form of every form that comes before it.” Elsewhere he says that the rational faculty governs the imaginative faculty and the chief sensory faculty—that is, the other faculties of the soul (p. 72). In another passage (p. 70), he says that the rational faculty is what allows us to grasp intelligible things, distinguish ugly from beautiful, and acquire crafts and sciences.↩︎

By “intelligibles,” al-Fārābī means “things whose nature is to be represented in the rational faculty. Some intelligibles are, in their own substances, actual intellects and actual intelligibles: these are things free of matter. Others are not in their own substances actually intelligible, such as stones and plants, and in general everything that is a body or is in a material body” (ibid., p. 82).↩︎

In the theory of emanation, the active intellect is the last of the ten intellects and the point at which emanation ends. Ontologically, it governs the world of earthly bodies. From the standpoint of knowledge, the active intellect “is a being whose substance is an actual intellect and is separate from matter (...) [and] gives the material intellect, which is intellect only potentially, something like the light that the sun gives to sight.” In other words, it is “what potential intelligibles need in order to move from potentiality to actuality” (same source, p. 83).↩︎

Al-Fārābī divides the rational faculty into theoretical and practical parts. “The practical was made to serve the theoretical, while the theoretical serves nothing else, but exists so that happiness may be reached through it. When happiness is known by the theoretical faculty, set up as a goal, desired by the appetitive faculty, and the deliberative faculty [thought] works out what should be done (...), and those actions are then carried out through the main powers of the appetitive faculty, all human actions become good and beautiful” (same source, pp. 86–87).↩︎

Many Qurʾānic verses say this. Among them are: “Your Lord surely knows what their hearts conceal and what they reveal” (Qurʾān 27:74); “Not even the weight of an atom in the heavens or the earth escapes Him” (34:3); “Not a leaf falls without His knowing it” (6:59); and “There is no private conversation among three people without Him being their fourth” (58:7), and so on.↩︎

We should point out that al-Fārābī and the other Arab philosophers who represent the rationalist current, like the Muslim theologians and Sufis, all begin from the principle of God’s oneness understood in terms of absolute transcendence. This is the fixed starting point they all share. Their differences lie in how they deal with the contradiction that arises between absolute transcendence and the ideological positions that force them to seek some connection between God and the world. In our view, this effort expressed their opposition to the theoretical foundation of the official ideology: the absolute separation of God from the world, which in reality reflected the principle of absolute separation between one human being and another—that is, between ruler and ruled. As we saw earlier, the Sufis establish a direct link between the world and God through unveiling and direct vision. The rationalist philosophers, by contrast, establish this link through intermediaries. The theory of emanation gave them the basis for these intermediaries—the separate intellects.↩︎
